catalog_quote: [Wilson 1969, sections 3-3.2, pp.89-90:] The materials presented in this section and in section 4 need considerably more work, but are presented here for the benefit of those interested. 3.1. STRESS. Stress occurs on the penult of poly-syllabic noun stems. Stress on verbs and affixed nouns has yet to be studied. 3.2. TONE. Pitch on words of more than three syllables has yet to be examined, but in a corpus of over 3000 words only the following contrastive word-tone patterns have been noted for words of up to three syllables: One syllable. High tone contrasts with low tone. ... Two syllables. High tone on the first syllable, low tone on the second contrasts with mid tone on the first syllable and low tone on the second. ... audit.reasoning: Quote check: all three deciding passages (Wilson 1969 sec.3-3.2 pp.89-90; SIL OPD 2004 p.3; Wilson 1974 p.10) are present verbatim in the held files at the stated places. Deciding source: a 1969 seven-page SIL phonology sketch by the language's only describer; its stress rule is one sentence ('Stress occurs on the penult of poly-syllabic noun stems'), explicitly preliminary, restricted to noun stems, with verbs 'yet to be studied' (1969) / 'more irregular' (OPD 2004), and the 169-pp 1974 grammar retreats to 'not fully analyzed as yet'. That is thin in substance, but it is the entire descriptive record: Glottolog's 5 refs are all Wilson and all held; the SIL [sue] resource list (10 items) is all Wilson/SIL; the two remaining Wilson items (1980 Zia-Suena comparative grammar, 1973/2008 dictionary) were fetched sources now and are silent on stress (dictionary adds only that tone is high vs mid, low

sources.citation: Wilson, Darryl. 1980 [web ed. 2008]. A brief comparative grammar of Zia and Suena. Ukarumpa: SIL. 67 pp. (SIL Language & Culture Archives 31220; scanned, no text layer; pp.1-18 scanned at 200 dpi one page at a time)
sources.quote: No stress statement. 'Zia and Suena share a common phonology, with the exception that Zia has five nasal vowels which Suena does not have, and Suena has two distinctive tones which Zia does not have. Since the practical orthography adopted for Suena does not symbolize tone, the Zia and Suena practical orthographies are identical...' Part I covers only word list, phoneme chart, Zia nasalization.
sources.locator: Part I.B 'Comparative chart of phonemes', PDF p.15 (scanned/)

sources.citation: Wilson, Darryl & Lael Wilson (compilers). 1973 [retyped 1977, web ed. 2008]. Suena-English Dictionary and English-Suena Dictionary. Ukarumpa: SIL. 87 pp. (SIL Language & Culture Archives 31122; text layer)
sources.quote: No stress statement. Tone: 'It is still uncertain what degree of functional load tone carries. There are about 40 minimal tone pairs that have been found to date. They have been noted here, using the SIL system of ́ to mark high tone, ̄ to mark mid tone, and ` to mark low tone. Only high and mid seem to contrast, as low occurs only word final (except for one syllable words). e.g. aménà parrot / ámenà backside'. Tone is marked on the minimal-pair headwords (e.g. atárà), so the dictionary is raw material for testing where the pitch peak sits on nouns, but it makes no claim about stress.
